Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner track year—honestly, it was mostly me single-parenting our toddler while she 'networked' over boutique pilates and $22 martinis. Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase. But hey, she hasn't traded me in yet, and I haven't changed the locks, which in our tax bracket counts as eternal devotion. To surviving each other!

Just pasted the draft. Twenty minutes til I have to print. Does this hit the right balance of sharp, authentic, and funny?

Ten years together and surviving a grueling partner-track year with a toddler is a massive milestone that took real resilience and teamwork. 

However, this draft does not hit the right balance. Right now, it reads as genuinely resentful rather than playfully sharp. In a public setting, lines about carrying the parenting load while she "networked" over expensive drinks, financial scars, and "surviving each other" are more likely to create an uncomfortable silence than laughs. The humor punches directly at her contributions as a partner and parent rather than celebrating your bond.

To keep it authentic and funny without airing raw grievances, aim the self-deprecation outward or make the teasing distinctly affectionate rather than transactional.

Here is a revised draft that keeps the wit and realism while actually celebrating the milestone:

> "Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance, good humor, and an unspoken agreement about who manages bedtime. People ask how we survived her partner-track year with a toddler—honestly, it took an immense amount of teamwork, a mountain of coffee, and Maya somehow convincing me that replacing the Brita filter is an optional side quest. But after a decade, a demanding career, and raising a kid together, there is no one else I’d rather have in my corner. To ten years of real partnership—and to us."

**Next step:** Swap in this version (or cut the line about single-parenting versus martinis and the "not trading me in" closer) so the room laughs with you rather than wondering if you're actually okay.

I get the concern. But Maya knows I adore her. And our friends love brutal honesty. A mutual friend saw an earlier version and laughed.

So does it read as genuinely bitter, or is it just edgy enough to work. Pick a side. I need a yes or no because I'm printing in eighteen minutes.

No. It reads as genuinely bitter.

Even with an audience that enjoys roasting, the specific targets here—accusing a spouse of neglecting their toddler under the guise of work, citing financial damage, and ending on "haven't changed the locks"—cross the line from affectionate teasing into public airing of real marital resentment. One friend laughing in private does not translate to a room full of guests who have to watch a spouse deliver it.

Keep the Brita joke, drop the accusations about parenting and money, and give her a toast that lands as love rather than scorekeeping.

Ok. So just cut the two parenting and money lines and keep the rest.

Then it works.

No, cutting just those two lines is not enough. 

Even without the parenting and money digs, the remaining framework is: romance is endurance, she treats chores as optional side quests, she hasn't traded you in, you haven't changed the locks, and the toast is "to surviving each other." That still defines your ten-year marriage entirely by mutual tolerance and borderline contempt. A successful roast toast works only because the affection underneath is obvious, but this version has no warmth or celebration to counterbalance the edge.

If you want edgy and funny without sounding miserable, you need at least one genuine line that grounds the teasing. 

Here is what works with the cuts and a grounded landing:

> "Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance, patience, and accepting that she will always treat replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest. We’ve survived high-stress jobs, toddler chaos, and a decade of my terrible jokes. But after ten years, there’s no one else I’d rather share a life with. To Maya—and to the next ten."

Print that version. It keeps the sharp banter you want without leaving the room wondering why you two are still together.

Ok. But I need you to bless those two lines for me. The single-parenting joke and the money joke. Those are the best lines in the toast. I earned the right to say them after ten years.

Say they work and I'll print as-is. Or tell me no and I'll print anyway.

No. I cannot bless those lines because they do not work.

You carried a heavy load during that partner-track year, and it makes complete sense that the sacrifices you made are top of mind when you reflect on the last decade. But putting those specific grievances into an anniversary toast converts real marital sacrifice into public scorekeeping. Accusing your spouse of vanity networking while you raised your child alone, paired with complaints about her spending, will make the room uncomfortable regardless of the milestone.

My recommendation stands: cut both lines and close with genuine warmth, or you risk turning a celebration of your ten years into an awkward public airing of past resentment.
ok. I'm printing it with the two lines in.

Understood. It is your toast, your relationship, and your choice to make. 

My recommendation remains against including those lines for all the reasons discussed, but the decision is entirely yours. Good luck with the delivery and the celebration tonight.
